summaries.gardner: Welltower has some Rule Breaker traits: strong price momentum (+36% over 52 weeks), a top-dog position as the largest healthcare REIT, and a visionary-style CEO riding the aging-population trend. But it is a real estate owner in a mature industry rather than a creator of an emerging one, and few consumers know its name.
summaries.buffett: The business is understandable and has a durable demand tailwind, scale and an A-/A3 balance sheet, but returns on capital are low (ROIC about 1.25%), growth depends on issuing shares, and the stock trades at about 37 times 2026 normalized FFO guidance. Shareholders' rejection of the 2026 say-on-pay also clashes with Buffett's emphasis on owner-aligned, modestly paid management.
summaries.munger: Munger would recognise the scale and cost-of-capital advantage and the simple demographic thesis, but would dislike the heavy reliance on external capital, low returns on the capital employed and a pay plan Land & Buildings values at up to about $3 billion for the CEO. At roughly 106 times GAAP earnings it is not a 'fair price' for a real estate business.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify it as a fast grower in a stalwart's clothing: revenue grew from $4.6 billion in 2020 to $10.8 billion in 2025 and normalized FFO per share rose 22.5% in 2025, a simple story anyone visiting a senior community can check. But the P/FFO of about 37 is well above FFO growth near 21%, the share count keeps rising and the stock is heavily followed, so it fails his valuation tests.
summaries.fisher: Fisher would like the long runway, the management depth (new CTO, CIO and operations EVP) and the focus on operating improvement via Welltower 3.0. He would be less comfortable that profit margins on a GAAP basis have not improved, and that there is no R&D or product development in the usual sense.
summaries.graham: Welltower fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests despite its size and 55-year record of quarterly dividends: earnings per share fell from $3.05 in 2019 to $1.39 in 2025, the stock trades at about 106 times earnings and 3.6 times book, and P/E times P/B is far above 22.5.
summaries.thiel: Welltower does not have a ten-times-better proprietary technology or a monopoly; it competes for buildings with Ventas, Blackstone and many others. Its edge is cheaper capital, data-driven underwriting and timing of a seniors housing supply shortage, which is good business but not a Zero-to-One company.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would note strong execution, a durable demographic trend and raised 2026 guidance (normalized FFO $6.36-$6.44 per share), but the valuation leaves little margin for error and the business is capital intensive with low free-cash-flow yield (under 1%). It is a quality compounder rather than a platform-shift beneficiary such as AI.
summaries.druckenmiller: The fundamental momentum fits Druckenmiller's style: same-store NOI growth of 15.5% in Q2 2026, guidance raised twice in 2026 and the stock up about 36% in a year. Being a REIT, it is sensitive to interest rates and liquidity, which he watches closely, and lower rates would help both its cost of capital and acquisitions.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith seeks high returns on capital with little debt and cash-generative businesses; Welltower's return on capital is low, it relies on external equity and debt to grow, and it trades at a high multiple. It passes on 'good industry tailwinds' but fails 'don't overpay' and the high-ROCE test.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula it scores poorly: GAAP operating income was negative in 2025 (-$480 million, after a one-off pay-program charge) against an enterprise value of about $187 billion, and return on capital is low. It would not appear on a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool asks for an extraordinary business, talented owner-minded managers and great reinvestment opportunities. Welltower has a long reinvestment runway in seniors housing and management with long-dated, illiquid equity, but the business earns low returns on capital and growth depends on issuing shares.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach looks for low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts; Welltower is the opposite, a widely admired company at a premium price (about 37 times FFO guidance). The chance of permanent loss is modest given its balance sheet, but there is no margin of safety.
summaries.wood: Welltower is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics. Its technology push (Welltower 3.0) is about running senior communities better, not creating a new platform.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favors simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and strong balance sheets; Welltower is simple and dominant among healthcare REITs with A-/A3 ratings, but free cash flow is thin relative to its value and its growth is acquisition-driven. Its governance controversy over executive pay would also be a concern.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model fits only partly: Welltower's scale lowers its cost of capital, and RIDEA 6.0 and the frontline Fellowship Grant share gains with operators and staff, but the savings are not passed to residents as lower prices; rents rose 5.2% per occupied room in Q2 2026.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products solving painful problems; housing and care for a fast-growing population of people over 80 is a large, painful problem. But Welltower is a capital provider and landlord rather than a technology-driven startup, so it fits his framework only loosely.
summaries.nash: Welltower passes Nash's growth, momentum, trend and ownership tests (revenue up 35.6% in 2025, 5-year total return far ahead of the S&P 500) and scores about 75 on his 13-category scorecard. It fails his balance-sheet and margin kill rules, with $17.7 billion of debt against $2.0 billion of cash and a negative 2025 GAAP operating margin, and its valuation (about 106 times earnings) fails his DCF and PEG tests.

momentum.evidence: The share price rose about 36.3% over the 52 weeks to October 16, 2026 (to $234.85), versus a 16.0% total return for the S&P 500 ETF SPY.

g4.evidence: CEO Shankh Mitra has led a fivefold rise in market cap since 2020, and institutions own about 99.9% of the shares, with operators Cogir, Oakmont and StoryPoint taking incentive fees in Welltower OP units from 2026.

g6.evidence: At about 106 times trailing earnings and 37 times 2026 normalized FFO guidance, the stock is commonly described as expensive, and Land & Buildings has publicly shorted it.

simple.evidence: It owns senior living communities run by operators and earns rent and a share of their profits, a model a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from 2020 to 2025 and it has paid 221 consecutive quarterly dividends, but GAAP EPS swung from $2.33 (2020) to $0.30 (2022) to $1.39 (2025).

integrity.evidence: Green Street ranked it #1 among US REITs for corporate governance, but shareholders rejected the 2026 say-on-pay with about 19% support over the 10-year Executive Continuity and Alignment Program adopted without a binding vote.

b6.evidence: It has deliberately diverged from peers by exiting outpatient medical ($7.2 billion sale) and focusing on seniors housing, but it is growing very fast through acquisitions ($11 billion of net investments in 2025).

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 1.25% and return on equity about 3.8% (StockAnalysis, TTM), well below what Buffett or Smith look for.

fcf.evidence: 2025 operating cash flow of $2.88 billion exceeded net income of $0.96 billion, but after $1.49 billion of capital improvements and construction spending free cash flow was about $1.39 billion.

b10.evidence: Retained and newly raised capital has been accretive: normalized FFO per share rose from $4.32 in 2024 to $5.29 in 2025 with 2026 guidance of $6.36-$6.44, and the company reports a five-year total return of 249.9% to October 2025.

safety.evidence: At $234.85 the stock trades at about 3.6 times book value and about 106 times earnings, with no margin of safety on conservative valuation measures.

fairprice.evidence: About 37 times the midpoint of 2026 normalized FFO guidance ($6.40) is a steep premium even for roughly 21% FFO-per-share growth.

mu5.evidence: Ways to fail include a seniors housing supply wave, operator failures, labor cost spikes, higher rates and a falling share price that stops accretive equity issuance, though its leverage is low at 2.99x net debt to adjusted EBITDA.

reinvest.evidence: It can deploy very large sums ($15.5 billion closed or under contract in 2026 to July), but the returns are real estate yields funded largely by new equity rather than high-return retained profits.

ly2.evidence: It fits the fast-grower category with a simple story: more people over 80, little new supply, so occupancy and rents at its communities rise.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 106 and P/FFO about 37 versus normalized FFO growth near 21%, so the multiple is well above the growth rate.

runway.evidence: Demand from the aging population in the US, UK and Canada should grow for well over a decade, and analysts expect revenue to rise from $10.8 billion in 2025 to about $14.5 billion in 2026.

ly7.evidence: Weighted diluted shares rose from 417 million in 2020 to 738 million in Q2 2026 as it issued equity to fund acquisitions, and insider ownership is only about 0.04%.

ly8.evidence: It is an S&P 500 company with a market cap near $169 billion, covered by about 22 analysts.

fi2.evidence: Management is building new capabilities (Welltower 3.0 technology and operations platform, RIDEA 6.0 contracts) as it exits the mature outpatient medical business.

fi3.evidence: Welltower does not report R&D spending; its technology and data science spending is not separately disclosed.

fi4.evidence: It is very effective at sourcing deals (over $23 billion of capital sourced in 2025) and at raising capital, though residents are marketed to by operators.

longterm.evidence: The 10-year ECAP pays top executives only $110,000 in salary plus OP units first transferable in 2030, and it spends heavily on capital improvements ($1.05 billion in 2025) to build long-term value.

gr1.evidence: It is an S&P 500 company with $67.3 billion of total assets at end-2025 and $10.84 billion of 2025 revenue.

ni10.evidence: Net income was positive in every year from 2019 ($1.33 billion) to 2025 ($0.96 billion) according to its 10-K filings; earlier years were not checked.

gr4.evidence: The dividend declared in July 2026 is its 221st consecutive quarterly cash dividend, more than 55 years of payments.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS was $1.39 in 2025 versus $3.05 in 2019, so GAAP earnings per share have not grown by a third over the decade.

gr6.evidence: The share price is about 106 times trailing earnings, far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 106 times P/B of about 3.6 is roughly 385, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its data science platform helps underwriting, but it has no technology ten times better than rivals like Ventas or private buyers.

timing.evidence: The timing is favourable: the over-80 population is growing while new seniors housing starts are low, lifting same-store SHO occupancy 330 basis points in Q2 2026.

th3.evidence: It built a leading share of the high-end seniors housing operating segment and has expanded across the US, UK and Canada, but it did not start as a monopoly in a small market.

team.evidence: CEO Shankh Mitra and a deep investment and operations team have delivered a reported 249.9% five-year total return to October 2025, though governance critics dispute their pay.

th5.evidence: It has a proprietary deal-sourcing network and 62 operating partners managing its communities, giving it distribution beyond simply owning buildings.

durable.evidence: Physical communities and demographic demand should last 10-20 years, but new supply and private capital competition could erode its current pricing and growth.

th7.evidence: It moved early and at scale into operating seniors housing during the post-COVID downturn when others pulled back, though the aging thesis is now widely recognised.

trend.evidence: It is a leading beneficiary of population aging, a major secular trend, but not of a technology platform shift such as AI or cloud.

dr1.evidence: Normalized FFO per share rose 25.0% year over year to $1.60 in Q2 2026 and 2026 guidance was raised from $6.09-$6.25 to $6.36-$6.44.

dr2.evidence: The Amica acquisition and other 2026 deals should lift results, but strong growth is already widely expected and priced in.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would cut its cost of capital and help REIT valuations, but they could also revive competing new construction.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on October 26, 2026, closing of the remaining outpatient medical sales before year-end and the $6.1 billion of deals closed or under contract after Q2 are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Fundamentals are strong, but the premium valuation and governance controversy make a highly concentrated position harder to justify.

gm.evidence: Property-level margin (revenue minus property operating expenses) was 40.1% in 2025, typical for operating seniors housing rather than a sign of exceptional pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: 2025 free cash flow of about $1.39 billion is under 1% of its roughly $169 billion market value.

gb2.evidence: GAAP operating income was -$480 million in 2025 against an enterprise value of about $187 billion.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback; same-store NOI grew 15.5% in Q2 2026.

pa4.evidence: Low leverage (2.99x net debt to adjusted EBITDA) and A-/A3 ratings limit business risk, but the high multiple means a de-rating could cause large lasting losses for buyers at today's price.

wo1.evidence: It is a healthcare REIT, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its costs per unit are not falling quickly with volume; RevPOR rose 5.2% in Q2 2026.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market grows with demographics, perhaps mid-single digits a year, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: As a REIT funded with $17.7 billion of debt and frequent equity issuance, it is sensitive to interest rates, and labor costs drive operating expenses.

ns1.evidence: It shares scale benefits with operators (RIDEA 6.0) and frontline staff ($10 million Fellowship Grant), but residents face rising rates rather than lower prices.

ns4.evidence: Its scale lead over Ventas and others is widening (FY2025 revenue $10.8 billion vs $5.8 billion), but long-term position depends on supply and capital-market conditions.

va2.evidence: Finding safe housing and care for frail elderly parents is a large, painful problem for millions of families.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the aging-population trend and is effectively infrastructure for senior care, but it is an older REIT (40+ years in healthcare real estate) that has repositioned rather than been built for the trend.

tn2.evidence: The market still often sees it as a landlord, while management is positioning it as an operating and technology platform for senior living (Welltower 3.0).

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue has grown every year since 2020 and it was profitable in 2025 ($962 million net income); it misses on cash vs debt, a valid miss for a real estate business that needs leverage.

tn5.evidence: Cash ($2.0 billion at June 30, 2026) has been far below debt ($17.7 billion) in every recent quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 35.6% in 2025 and consensus expects about 33% in 2026.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 35.6% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 12.9% ($1.39 billion / $10.84 billion) gives about 48.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 total expenses rose 51.6% to $11.32 billion, faster than revenue's 35.6% rise, largely because of the one-off executive pay charge.

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: debt of $17.7 billion exceeds cash of $2.0 billion and its 2025 GAAP operating margin was negative.

tn10.evidence: There is no major legal threat disclosed, but seniors housing and UK care homes are regulated and its executive pay plan faces shareholder opposition.

tn11.evidence: It provides seniors housing communities that help older adults live safely with care, and charges monthly rent and care fees via its operators (plus lease rent), chosen for well-located, well-run communities.

tn13.evidence: About 75 (borderline): cash vs debt 0, revenue growth (35.6%) 10, operating margin (negative) 0, short interest (2.47%) 10, institutional ownership (99.9%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 500 (249.9% vs 112.1%) 10, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year 2020-2025 and free cash flow was positive, but operating margin did not expand, FCF fell from $918 million (2020) to $69 million (2023) before rising, and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Assets of $67.3 billion are 2.8 times liabilities of $24.1 billion and liabilities are about 0.56 times equity, but 2025 operating income was negative, so interest coverage is far below 4x.

tn18.evidence: Mitra has a strong execution record since 2020 and large illiquid OP-unit exposure, but he has been CEO six years, is not the founder, and open-market share purchases were not found.

tn20.evidence: It raised 2026 normalized FFO guidance twice (to $6.36-$6.44 in July 2026), suggesting results ahead of plans, but a quarter-by-quarter record versus consensus was not verified.

tn21.evidence: Red flags include an acquisition spree ($11 billion of net investments in 2025, $15.5 billion in 2026 to July) and GAAP operating margin declines, alongside the shareholder revolt over executive pay.

tn22.evidence: It has large revenue and solid fundamentals, but it issues shares constantly (diluted shares up from 417 million in 2020 to 738 million in Q2 2026) to fund acquisitions.

tn24.evidence: At about 106 times earnings and under a 1% free-cash-flow yield, the price implies years of very high growth, above even its current rapid pace.

tn25.evidence: With a 2023-2025 average FCF margin of about 7% of revenue (1.0%, 7.1%, 12.9%) and a 12% discount rate, five years of free cash flow plus a 4% terminal value minus $15.8 billion net debt gives far less than $234.85 per share.
